PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Supporters: The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn Opponents: ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.
CON
No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.

### Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's office on July 16, 2025.
The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025.
To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment.
The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements.
The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Voter Identification
Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Voter Identification
Registered Voter List Administration Initiative
Summary
Proposition 39 began as a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment filed with the California Attorney General's (https://oag.ca.gov/) office on July 16, 2025. The initiative received a revised ballot title and was approved for signature gathering on September 19, 2025. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 874,641 valid signatures.The campaign submitted nearly 1.37 million signatures on March 2, 2026 and the initiative officially qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 39 on April 24, 2026.
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID (https://www.voteridca.org/) filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment. The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements. The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions. On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections. State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county. Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot. In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification. Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information. The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year. Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs by an estimated tens of millions to the low hundreds of millions of dollars annually, although the exact amount would depend on how the measure is implemented. These costs amount to less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Major costs would be influenced by decisions about the new voter identification card, administrative requirements, and the number of voters requesting cards. As ineligible voters or eligible voters lack the required identification are removed from voting, some savings could result.
What your vote means
YES: A "yes" vote supports amending the state constitution to require government-issued ID for in-person voting or the last four digits of a designated government ID for mail-in voting, mandate annual citizenship-verification reporting for county voter rolls, and require odd-year compliance audits by the State Auditor.
NO: A "no" vote opposes these changes, maintaining current law where government ID is not required to vote, and voters attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury without requiring election officials to verify attestations against government data or report verification rates.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters of Proposition 39 argue that requiring voter identification would strengthen confidence in California elections by adding safeguards they believe are currently lacking. They point to voter ID requirements in other states and countries as evidence that such rules are a common feature of democratic election systems rather than an unusual restriction. Supporters also contend that changes such as universal mail ballots and ballot collection have increased the need for additional identity checks. While they do not necessarily claim that widespread voter fraud is occurring, they maintain that Proposition 39 would make the election process more secure, transparent, and less vulnerable to public doubt.
Opponents of Proposition 39 argue that the measure would impose unnecessary barriers on eligible voters without addressing a demonstrated problem in California elections. They contend that existing procedures already provide multiple safeguards for verifying voters and that additional identification and citizenship checks could lead to eligible ballots being rejected, with disproportionate effects on people with disabilities and others who may have difficulty meeting the new requirements.
Critics also raise privacy concerns about placing partial identification numbers on mail ballot envelopes and argue that implementing the measure would create significant new administrative costs. Finally, opponents characterize Proposition 39 as part of a national push for stricter voting rules that they believe would make voting more difficult rather than meaningfully improve election security.

**Proposition 39**, also known as the **California voter ID initiative**, is an initiated constitutional amendment in the state of California that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot.
The initiative would amend the state constitution to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a mail-in ballot.
The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the secretary of state and election officials.
If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.

Proposition 39 would require voters to show a government-issued ID when voting in person or provide the last four digits of an ID on mail ballots. Proposition 39 would require voters to show a government-issued ID when voting in person or provide the last four digits of an ID on mail ballots. It would also require election officials to use government data to verify citizenship when possible, report verification rates and undergo state audits of election procedures.
A “no” vote would keep current rules, which do not require voter ID at the polls or government-data checks of citizenship attestations.

Editorial Standards ⓘ (https://www.ksbw.com/article/hearst-television-news-policy-statements/14471973)
Brian Wiechert
Digital Content Manager
Voters across the country are beginning to head to the polls Tuesday to decide control of both chambers of Congress and elect dozens of governors, along with state and local officials. Follow live updates here throughout the day.
Thirty-five U.S. Senate seats are up for election, as Democrats need a net four seats to win control. To obtain this majority, Democrats must win multiple states that President Donald Trump won – some by double digits – in 2024.
Advertisement
Additionally, 435 U.S. House contests are up for grabs. Democrats will need a net gain of three seats to take back the House, a task that was complicated by Republican redistricting.
Thirty-six governor seats are also up for election, with several competitive contests clustered in presidential battlegrounds. Here's where the balance of power stands.
SENATE RACES TO WATCH
Control of the U.S. Senate is up for grabs. And Republicans increasingly find themselves on defense as they try to hold on to their majority in the chamber.
The political winds are swirling against President Donald Trump and Republicans, as they historically do in midterm elections for the party in power.
Senate Republicans were optimistic going into the election thanks in large part to the map.
Currently, the GOP holds a 53-47 majority.
Thirty-five seats are up for reelection: Republicans hold 22, while Democrats hold 13. With Republican Vice President JD Vance’s ability to break tie votes, Democrats need 51 seats to win control of the chamber.
Here is what that uphill path to power looks like for Democrats.
The most straightforward path for Democrats to win the majority involves holding all of their seats, including the battlegrounds of Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire.
On top of that, they will need to pick up four more seats, and their best opportunities are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.
The challenge for Democrats is that besides Maine, Trump won all of those pickup targets in 2016, 2020 and 2024. To win back the upper chamber, Democrats will have to persuade a significant number of voters who cast ballots for Trump over the last decade to vote for the opposing party this time.
Which races could determine control of Congress? (https://www.ksbw.com/article/five-days-until-midterms-which-races-could-determine-control-congress/74280590)
Here is a breakdown of the big Senate races to watch (https://www.ksbw.com/article/key-senate-races-2026-midterm-election/74265586).
HOUSE RACES TO WATCH
Voters in all 435 congressional districts are choosing their representatives, and the results will determine which party controls the U.S. House. A small number of closely contested races could decide the balance of power.
The contest is unfolding on new district maps in several states after an unusual round of mid-decade redistricting. Those changes have reshaped some races and added another layer to a fight that was already expected to be close.
The magic number to win the majority of seats in the House is 218.
Going into Election Day, 219 House members caucus with Republicans, leaving the party with little room for losses if it hopes to retain control.
That narrow margin could be vulnerable in a midterm election. Historically, the president’s party has often lost House seats in midterms, though each election brings its own dynamics.
With races playing out across the country, tracking the fight district by district can be difficult.
The Cook Political Report is a nonpartisan publication that analyzes and rates U.S. elections and political races. It has rated 53 House races as competitive: 18 lean Democratic, 17 lean Republican and 18 are toss-ups.
The interactive map below details what's at stake.
KEY GOVERNOR RACES TO WATCH
Thirty-six states have gubernatorial contests on the ballot this year.
Ahead of Election Day, there were 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors.
With 19 incumbents leaving office, there will be a lot of turnover – and an opportunity for Democrats to hold a majority of the posts for the first time since 2010.
The races will also test whether Democrats can capitalize on a midterm environment that has put several Republican-held seats in play. Some campaigns have grown especially bitter, with personal attacks and family history pulled into the fight.
The most competitive contests will offer an early read on both parties’ strength ahead of the 2028 presidential race.
Below are some of the top races to watch in 2026.

...
### Summary
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections.
State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county.
Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot.
In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification.
Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year.
Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.

Voters across the country are beginning to head to the polls Tuesday to decide control of both chambers of Congress and elect dozens of governors, along with state and local officials. Follow live updates here throughout the day.
Thirty-five U.S. Senate seats are up for election, as Democrats need a net four seats to win control. To obtain this majority, Democrats must win multiple states that President Donald Trump won – some by double digits – in 2024.
Advertisement
Additionally, 435 U.S. House contests are up for grabs. Democrats will need a net gain of three seats to take back the House, a task that was complicated by Republican redistricting.
Thirty-six governor seats are also up for election, with several competitive contests clustered in presidential battlegrounds. Here's where the balance of power stands.
SENATE RACES TO WATCH
Control of the U.S. Senate is up for grabs. And Republicans increasingly find themselves on defense as they try to hold on to their majority in the chamber.
The political winds are swirling against President Donald Trump and Republicans, as they historically do in midterm elections for the party in power.
Senate Republicans were optimistic going into the election thanks in large part to the map.
Currently, the GOP holds a 53-47 majority.
Thirty-five seats are up for reelection: Republicans hold 22, while Democrats hold 13. With Republican Vice President JD Vance’s ability to break tie votes, Democrats need 51 seats to win control of the chamber.
Here is what that uphill path to power looks like for Democrats.
The most straightforward path for Democrats to win the majority involves holding all of their seats, including the battlegrounds of Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire.
On top of that, they will need to pick up four more seats, and their best opportunities are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.
The challenge for Democrats is that besides Maine, Trump won all of those pickup targets in 2016, 2020 and 2024. To win back the upper chamber, Democrats will have to persuade a significant number of voters who cast ballots for Trump over the last decade to vote for the opposing party this time.
Which races could determine control of Congress? (https://www.ksbw.com/article/five-days-until-midterms-which-races-could-determine-control-congress/74280590)
Here is a breakdown of the big Senate races to watch (https://www.ksbw.com/article/key-senate-races-2026-midterm-election/74265586).
HOUSE RACES TO WATCH
Voters in all 435 congressional districts are choosing their representatives, and the results will determine which party controls the U.S. House. A small number of closely contested races could decide the balance of power.
The contest is unfolding on new district maps in several states after an unusual round of mid-decade redistricting. Those changes have reshaped some races and added another layer to a fight that was already expected to be close.
The magic number to win the majority of seats in the House is 218.
Going into Election Day, 219 House members caucus with Republicans, leaving the party with little room for losses if it hopes to retain control.
That narrow margin could be vulnerable in a midterm election. Historically, the president’s party has often lost House seats in midterms, though each election brings its own dynamics.
With races playing out across the country, tracking the fight district by district can be difficult.
The Cook Political Report is a nonpartisan publication that analyzes and rates U.S. elections and political races. It has rated 53 House races as competitive: 18 lean Democratic, 17 lean Republican and 18 are toss-ups.
The interactive map below details what's at stake.
KEY GOVERNOR RACES TO WATCH
Thirty-six states have gubernatorial contests on the ballot this year.
Ahead of Election Day, there were 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors.
With 19 incumbents leaving office, there will be a lot of turnover – and an opportunity for Democrats to hold a majority of the posts for the first time since 2010.
The races will also test whether Democrats can capitalize on a midterm environment that has put several Republican-held seats in play. Some campaigns have grown especially bitter, with personal attacks and family history pulled into the fight.
The most competitive contests will offer an early read on both parties’ strength ahead of the 2028 presidential race.

Live updates: Voters begin casting ballots as key races could reshape the nation
Updated: 5:29 AM PST Nov 3, 2026
Editorial Standards ⓘ (https://www.ksbw.com/article/hearst-television-news-policy-statements/14471973)
Brian Wiechert
Digital Content Manager
Voters across the country are beginning to head to the polls Tuesday to decide control of both chambers of Congress and elect dozens of governors, along with state and local officials. Follow live updates here throughout the day.
Thirty-five U.S. Senate seats are up for election, as Democrats need a net four seats to win control. To obtain this majority, Democrats must win multiple states that President Donald Trump won – some by double digits – in 2024.
Advertisement
Additionally, 435 U.S. House contests are up for grabs. Democrats will need a net gain of three seats to take back the House, a task that was complicated by Republican redistricting.
Thirty-six governor seats are also up for election, with several competitive contests clustered in presidential battlegrounds. Here's where the balance of power stands.
SENATE RACES TO WATCH
Control of the U.S. Senate is up for grabs. And Republicans increasingly find themselves on defense as they try to hold on to their majority in the chamber.
The political winds are swirling against President Donald Trump and Republicans, as they historically do in midterm elections for the party in power.
Senate Republicans were optimistic going into the election thanks in large part to the map.
Currently, the GOP holds a 53-47 majority.
Thirty-five seats are up for reelection: Republicans hold 22, while Democrats hold 13. With Republican Vice President JD Vance’s ability to break tie votes, Democrats need 51 seats to win control of the chamber.
Here is what that uphill path to power looks like for Democrats.
The most straightforward path for Democrats to win the majority involves holding all of their seats, including the battlegrounds of Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire.
On top of that, they will need to pick up four more seats, and their best opportunities are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.
The challenge for Democrats is that besides Maine, Trump won all of those pickup targets in 2016, 2020 and 2024. To win back the upper chamber, Democrats will have to persuade a significant number of voters who cast ballots for Trump over the last decade to vote for the opposing party this time.
Which races could determine control of Congress? (https://www.ksbw.com/article/five-days-until-midterms-which-races-could-determine-control-congress/74280590)
Here is a breakdown of the big Senate races to watch (https://www.ksbw.com/article/key-senate-races-2026-midterm-election/74265586).
HOUSE RACES TO WATCH
Voters in all 435 congressional districts are choosing their representatives, and the results will determine which party controls the U.S. House. A small number of closely contested races could decide the balance of power.
The contest is unfolding on new district maps in several states after an unusual round of mid-decade redistricting. Those changes have reshaped some races and added another layer to a fight that was already expected to be close.
The magic number to win the majority of seats in the House is 218.
Going into Election Day, 219 House members caucus with Republicans, leaving the party with little room for losses if it hopes to retain control.
That narrow margin could be vulnerable in a midterm election. Historically, the president’s party has often lost House seats in midterms, though each election brings its own dynamics.
With races playing out across the country, tracking the fight district by district can be difficult.
The Cook Political Report is a nonpartisan publication that analyzes and rates U.S. elections and political races. It has rated 53 House races as competitive: 18 lean Democratic, 17 lean Republican and 18 are toss-ups.
The interactive map below details what's at stake.
KEY GOVERNOR RACES TO WATCH
Thirty-six states have gubernatorial contests on the ballot this year.
Ahead of Election Day, there were 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors.
With 19 incumbents leaving office, there will be a lot of turnover – and an opportunity for Democrats to hold a majority of the posts for the first time since 2010.
The races will also test whether Democrats can capitalize on a midterm environment that has put several Republican-held seats in play. Some campaigns have grown especially bitter, with personal attacks and family history pulled into the fight.
The most competitive contests will offer an early read on both parties’ strength ahead of the 2028 presidential race.

## Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
...
### Summary
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections.
State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county.
Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.
The measure would also require voters to provide identifying information each time they cast a ballot.
In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification.
Elections officials would confirm that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.The State Auditor would review state and county compliance every odd numbered year.
Proposition 39 mandates that the Legislature would need to clarify details not included in the proposition and they would have to pass additional laws before the measure could be fully implemented.

## Opponents argue this initiative adds costly, unnecessary hurdles that will block eligible citizens from casting ballots
**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...**
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID.
It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.

Voters across the country are beginning to head to the polls Tuesday to decide control of both chambers of Congress and elect dozens of governors, along with state and local officials. Follow live updates here throughout the day.
Thirty-five U.S. Senate seats are up for election, as Democrats need a net four seats to win control. To obtain this majority, Democrats must win multiple states that President Donald Trump won – some by double digits – in 2024.
Advertisement
Additionally, 435 U.S. House contests are up for grabs. Democrats will need a net gain of three seats to take back the House, a task that was complicated by Republican redistricting.
Thirty-six governor seats are also up for election, with several competitive contests clustered in presidential battlegrounds. Here's where the balance of power stands.
SENATE RACES TO WATCH
Control of the U.S. Senate is up for grabs. And Republicans increasingly find themselves on defense as they try to hold on to their majority in the chamber.
The political winds are swirling against President Donald Trump and Republicans, as they historically do in midterm elections for the party in power.
Senate Republicans were optimistic going into the election thanks in large part to the map.
Currently, the GOP holds a 53-47 majority.
Thirty-five seats are up for reelection: Republicans hold 22, while Democrats hold 13. With Republican Vice President JD Vance’s ability to break tie votes, Democrats need 51 seats to win control of the chamber.
Here is what that uphill path to power looks like for Democrats.
The most straightforward path for Democrats to win the majority involves holding all of their seats, including the battlegrounds of Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire.
On top of that, they will need to pick up four more seats, and their best opportunities are in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.
The challenge for Democrats is that besides Maine, Trump won all of those pickup targets in 2016, 2020 and 2024. To win back the upper chamber, Democrats will have to persuade a significant number of voters who cast ballots for Trump over the last decade to vote for the opposing party this time.

HOUSE RACES TO WATCH
Voters in all 435 congressional districts are choosing their representatives, and the results will determine which party controls the U.S. House. A small number of closely contested races could decide the balance of power.
The contest is unfolding on new district maps in several states after an unusual round of mid-decade redistricting. Those changes have reshaped some races and added another layer to a fight that was already expected to be close.
The magic number to win the majority of seats in the House is 218.
Going into Election Day, 219 House members caucus with Republicans, leaving the party with little room for losses if it hopes to retain control.
That narrow margin could be vulnerable in a midterm election. Historically, the president’s party has often lost House seats in midterms, though each election brings its own dynamics.
With races playing out across the country, tracking the fight district by district can be difficult.
The Cook Political Report is a nonpartisan publication that analyzes and rates U.S. elections and political races. It has rated 53 House races as competitive: 18 lean Democratic, 17 lean Republican and 18 are toss-ups.

KEY GOVERNOR RACES TO WATCH
Thirty-six states have gubernatorial contests on the ballot this year.
Ahead of Election Day, there were 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors.
With 19 incumbents leaving office, there will be a lot of turnover – and an opportunity for Democrats to hold a majority of the posts for the first time since 2010.
The races will also test whether Democrats can capitalize on a midterm environment that has put several Republican-held seats in play. Some campaigns have grown especially bitter, with personal attacks and family history pulled into the fight.
The most competitive contests will offer an early read on both parties’ strength ahead of the 2028 presidential race.

Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections.
State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county.
Voters would also have to select a government-issued form of identification when registering in order to vote by mail, and the state would provide a free voter identification card to anyone who requests one.

In-person voters would need to present government-issued identification, while mail voters would provide the last four digits of their selected identification number on the ballot envelope for verification.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. 

If it passes, Proposition 40 would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Californians vote on nation’s first wealth tax on billionaires

By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. 

If it passes, Proposition 40 would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. 

Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. I'm also weighing the polls against the money on each side, since the No side is well funded while Yes has roughly $24M to $36M. The recent polls range widely, with most showing No ahead, though a few show Yes close or leading. My rough read is that the average leans No.

I'm pulling the full poll list next, since the averages drift a few points depending on which surveys are included. I also want the late October polls, including Berkeley IGS, PPIC, and any Emerson, Politico, or LA Times releases. I'm weighing whether "which side wins" means the Yes side or the No side, since a single yes or no only makes sense once that's fixed. Reading it as whether Yes is favored, the polling points to no.

I'm weighing whether the question means the Yes side (the proposition's side) or the No side, since a yes or no answer only makes sense once that's pinned down. The most natural reading is whether the Yes side is more likely to win, so I'm leaning toward that framing.

I'm settling on a single reading of the question. Since the page is about the proposition, I'll treat "Yes" as the side backing it, and the polling suggests that side isn't favored to win.

I'm now weighing whether a bare yes or no can really answer "which side," since it only works once one side is fixed. The page is about Prop 39, so the most natural reading is whether the Yes side will win, and with the polls leaning No, that points to no.

I'm checking whether the election has already happened, since the latest pages I've seen were cached before polls closed on November 3. If results are in, the answer should match the actual outcome rather than the pre-election polling.

I'm checking whether any Prop 39 or governor results have come in after Election Day, since the cached pages I've seen predate the polls closing. I also want the historical record on voter ID ballot measures, since several states have passed them and a few have failed.

I'm recalling which states have passed voter ID ballot measures and which have failed, along with the rough vote margins, to see how those outcomes compare with this one. I'm also thinking about how California's own past voter ID fights have gone, but the main question is still California itself.

Next I'm weighing how Prop 39's chances look against California's partisan makeup and the current political environment. Democrats are strongly opposed, Republicans are nearly unanimous in support, and independents lean slightly yes, so the measure looks unlikely to pass in a midterm favoring Democrats.

I'm recalling how past ballot measures that began with majority opposition have fared, since they usually lose, and how support tends to erode. The Berkeley IGS numbers show a yes side slipping from roughly No +9 in August to No +20 in October, with undecided voters likely breaking toward No.

I'm going to check the campaign finance totals next, comparing the spending on each side, and then look at the Wikipedia polling table and whether any post-election results have come in.

'''Proposition 39''', also known as the '''California voter ID initiative''', is an [[initiated constitutional amendment]] in the state of [[California]] that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot. The initiative would amend the [[Constitution of California|state constitution]] to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a [[mail-in ballot]]. 

The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the [[California secretary of state|secretary of state]] and election officials. If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.

== Background ==
Currently, the [[Constitution of California|state constitution]] limits voting to [[U.S. citizens]], though [[proof of citizenship]] is not required unless a voter has become a U.S. citizen less than 15 days before an election. During the voter registration process, individuals must provide a form of ID and attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of [[perjury]].<ref name="Perjury">{{cite web |title=Voter Registration |url=https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration |website=Secretary of State of California |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> California is one of only 14 U.S. states that does not require identification while voting on [[Election Day (United States)|election day]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Voter identification laws by state |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state |website=Ballotpedia |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 

On April 24, 2026, state officials announced that the initiative had qualified for the November ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures.<ref name="Proponents"/><ref name="SFist">{{cite web |title=Republican-Backed California Voter ID Measure Makes It On November Ballot |url=https://sfist.com/2026/04/28/republican-backed-california-voter-id-measure-makes-it-on-november-ballot/ |website=SFist |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en |date=28 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260429093012/https://sfist.com/2026/04/28/republican-backed-california-voter-id-measure-makes-it-on-november-ballot/ |archive-date=April 29, 2026 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="CalMat">{{cite web |last1=Lathan |first1=Nadia |title=A Republican-backed push for voter ID gains momentum in California |url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/03/california-voter-id-initiative/ |website=CalMatters |access-date=29 April 2026 |date=10 March 2026}}</ref>

Three other states – [[2026 Nevada Question 7|Nevada]], [[2026 North Carolina Require Voter Identification Amendment|North Carolina]], and [[Oklahoma]] – will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots.<ref name="Bal12345">{{cite web |title=California Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative (2026) |url=https://ballotpedia.org/California_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026) |website=Ballotpedia |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en |date=9 April 2026}}</ref>

=== Impact ===
The initiative would amend the state constitution to enforce the use of government-issued ID while voting in-person, and the use of the last four digits of a government-issued ID number when [[mail-in ballot|voting by mail]].<ref name="Proponents"/> Additionally, it would mandate the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the [[California secretary of state|secretary of state]] and county election officials, and require the state of California to provide free ID cards upon request to voters casting a ballot.<ref name="Proponents"/>

The voter ID initiative would also authorize the [[California legislature]] to enact laws that would force compliance with the amendment, and permit citizens to seek judicial review if they feel the state of California or any county within it is failing to comply with the amendment.<ref name="Chill"/> Additionally, the [[California State Auditor|state auditor]] would be required to publicly audit state and county compliance every second year.<ref name="Chill">{{cite web |title=California's Voter ID Initiative is Way More Chill Than Trump's SAVE Act |url=https://ivn.us/posts/californias-voter-id-initiative-is-way-more-chill-than-trumps-save-act-2026-03-10 |website=Independent Voter News |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en |date=10 March 2026}}</ref>

'''Proposition 39''', also known as the '''California voter ID initiative''', is an [[initiated constitutional amendment]] in the state of [[California]] that on November 3, 2026, will be on the ballot. The initiative would amend the [[Constitution of California|state constitution]] to require the use of a government-issued ID for in-person voting, as well as the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number when casting a [[mail-in ballot]]. 

The amendment would also require the state of California to provide free voter ID cards that can be used to cast a ballot, and would enforce the maintenance of accurate voter registration lists by the [[California secretary of state|secretary of state]] and election officials. If approved, the amendment would make California the 37th U.S. state to require voter ID during elections, and the 10th U.S. state to support a voter ID ballot measure.

== Background ==
Currently, the [[Constitution of California|state constitution]] limits voting to [[U.S. citizens]], though [[proof of citizenship]] is not required unless a voter has become a U.S. citizen less than 15 days before an election. During the voter registration process, individuals must provide a form of ID and attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of [[perjury]].<ref name="Perjury">{{cite web |title=Voter Registration |url=https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration |website=Secretary of State of California |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> California is one of only 14 U.S. states that does not require identification while voting on [[Election Day (United States)|election day]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Voter identification laws by state |url=https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state |website=Ballotpedia |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en}}</ref> 

On April 24, 2026, state officials announced that the initiative had qualified for the November ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures.<ref name="Proponents"/><ref name="SFist">{{cite web |title=Republican-Backed California Voter ID Measure Makes It On November Ballot |url=https://sfist.com/2026/04/28/republican-backed-california-voter-id-measure-makes-it-on-november-ballot/ |website=SFist |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en |date=28 April 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260429093012/https://sfist.com/2026/04/28/republican-backed-california-voter-id-measure-makes-it-on-november-ballot/ |archive-date=April 29, 2026 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="CalMat">{{cite web |last1=Lathan |first1=Nadia |title=A Republican-backed push for voter ID gains momentum in California |url=https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/03/california-voter-id-initiative/ |website=CalMatters |access-date=29 April 2026 |date=10 March 2026}}</ref>

Three other states – [[2026 Nevada Question 7|Nevada]], [[2026 North Carolina Require Voter Identification Amendment|North Carolina]], and [[Oklahoma]] – will also see voter ID measures on their November 2026 ballots.<ref name="Bal12345">{{cite web |title=California Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative (2026) |url=https://ballotpedia.org/California_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026) |website=Ballotpedia |access-date=29 April 2026 |language=en |date=9 April 2026}}</ref>
